newsitem.title: USA: Republicans, eager to leave, ease pursestrings.
newsitem.headline: Republicans, eager to leave, ease pursestrings.

text.p: The Republican-led Congress will give President Clinton more money for his cherished domestic programs than it seemed possible last year when lawmakers shut the government rather than meet his request.
Six weeks before the Nov. 5 election, Republicans admit they are unwilling to risk a bruising battle with Clinton over spending cuts in education, job training and law enforcement.

Last year, the heady atmosphere of new power after 40 years in the minority led to a showdown with Democrat Clinton over domestic programs. It resulted in two federal shutdowns that polls showed the public mostly blamed on Republicans.

This year, Republicans have their sights on leaving town to campaign in hopes of holding on to their majority status. Their presidential candidate Bob Dole lags in the polls and Democratic candidates across the country are hoping to ride Clinton's coattails to reclaim Congress.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, R-Ga., said Friday he did not want politics to interfere with these must-pass spending bills -- or with their leaving Washington to campaign.

"We think that it is better in this political environment to go ahead and get the legislation done. Then, let the Congress go out and let the president go out and have the political campaigning rather than have politics interfere directly in the legislative process," he said.

Scarcely were the words out of Gingrich's mouth before Democrats called foul, charging that his offer was full of politics. Republicans sought to bring the spending bill to a vote under procedures that would make Democratic amendments difficult, if not impossible, to win.

Gingrich and Senate leaders told reporters they could accept Clinton's domestic spending request, which included more than $2 billion for education, if the president would back off his call for $3.5 billion in defense spending cuts.

Essentially, Republicans have agreed to add nearly $3 billion to education in 1997 after agreeing earlier in the year to hold education funding steady next year. The deep cuts in education came in 1995.
"Our negotiations are aimed at providing the extra $5 billion to $6 billion that he has requested," said House Appropriations Committee chairman Bob Livingston, R-La.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle told reporters Friday: "That's a non-starter." The South Dakota Democrat also objected to Republican Leader Trent Lott's offer that each side be permitted only six amendments.

In this more sobering atmosphere, Republicans agreed last week to give Clinton about $6 billion more on a nearly $600 billion spending bill that must pass by Oct. 1 when the government's new fiscal year starts. This bill would pay for the departments of Defense, Justice, Commerce, Health and Human Services, Education, Labor, State, Interior and Treasury, the White House and numerous federal agencies.
They also agreed to restore some of the money cut last year from housing programs and environmental protection as part of another $85 billion bill that also helps veterans.
They backed off a House plan to kill Clinton's prized AmeriCorps youth service program.
And, earlier this month, the Republican Congress boosted funds for transportation, energy and water programs by nearly $1.5 billion.

In addition to money for job training, education and other programs, Clinton's request includes a special $1.1 billion increase in the effort to fight terrorism, some of which will go to add protection for U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia and other countries. It also would pay $500 million to aid in fighting forest fires in Western states and add $250 million to the government's work to combat illegal drugs.

But as Livingston noted, rather than increase deficit to pay for these emergency requests, Congress will pay for it this year -- by selling broadcast airwave rights and forcing savings and loans to add money to their reserve fund.
The appropriations bill, known as a continuing resolution, is regarded as the last legislative train to leave the station this year. Many members are eager to add election-year projects to its cars.
